title: FAST '26 - PolarStore: High-Performance Data Compression for Large-Scale Cloud-Native Databases
transcriptText:
Hi everyone. I'm Jinrui from Alibaba
Cloud. Today I will present our work
Polar Store high-performance data
compression for large-scale cloud cloud
native database.
I will introduce the background and the
motivation.
Let me start with the background. Polar
DB is a cloud native relational
database. It uses storage computer
separate architecture. In this
architecture, we have a read write node
that handles write requests, multiple
read only nodes for read queries, and a
shared storage layer at the bottom. The
key benefits of this architecture is
that elastic computing scaling. Users
can scale computing resources up and
down without any data migration. This
significantly reduces computing cost.
However, storage cost is a remain
critical concern for our users,
especially during periods of low
activity.
Therefore, data compression becomes
effective way to reduce this storage
cost.
From our users' perspective, there are
two main concerns about the compression.
First, compression ratio. Users want the
highest highest possible compression to
save money. For cold data and snapshots,
they want to even higher ratio.
Second, the performance. Users cannot
tolerate any degradation on latency
latency sensitive operations.
Specifically, redo log write and
the page read latency.
And importantly, compression should not
consume extra CPU resources on computer
node because these resources are billed
to users. So, our question is how to do
it achieve a high compression ratio
without any performance overhead.
There are three key dimensions to
consider.
The first is the compression input input
size. This means how much data we feed
into the compressor at a time. The
second is the compression algorithm.
This
ranges from lightweight algorithm like
LZ4 to heavy algorithm like gzip.
The third is the index granularity. To
understand this, think of the space
before compression as the logical space
and the space after compression as the
physical space. With compression, the
system needs to maintain
index that maps the logical space to the
physical locations.
The index granularity defines the
smallest unit that mapping.
In other words, it defines the smallest
piece of compressed data that can be
independently located and read.
For the compression input block size, a
larger block block gives a compression
algorithm more information to work with,
so it achieves a higher compression
ratio, but it also introduces extra
amplification and extra compression and
or decompression overhead.
On the other hand,
a smaller block enables better random
access, but gives a lower compression
ratio. This is a foundational trade-off
between compression ratio and
performance.
The second dimension is the compression
algorithm. Software based approach
offers flexible compression parameters
and dynamic configurations, but they
come with lower performance.
Hardware based approach like FPGA or QAT
provide a high performance, but they are
limited to fixed configurations. Again,
this is a trade-off between compression
ratio and performance.
The third dimension is the index
granularity. Byte level indexing is a
space efficient, but it requires complex
garbage collection and space management.
4 kilobyte level
indexing is simple, but it wastes
space compared to byte level indexing.
This is another difficult trade-off
between compression ratio and
performance.
Now, let me show the exciting approaches
in original Polar DB.
The first one is B+ tree compression at
the database layer.
It takes
16 kilobyte input,
uses flexible software compression, but
index at 4 kilobyte
granularity. The problem The problem is
that the 4 kilobyte indexing leads to
space fragmentation and sub-optimal
compression ratio.
The second approach uses computational
storage drives or CSD.
CSD compresses 4 kilobyte input block
and user level and uses byte level
indexing handled by the variable
variable length FTL. It achieves
extended space efficiency with zero
software overhead. However,
the input size is fixed at 4 kilobyte
and the compression algorithm is not a
flexible. Therefore, neither approach
can break the trade-off.
This brings our key idea, dual layer
compression.
As shown in the figure,
layer one is the software layer. It
compresses 16 kilobyte pages into
unblocks.
It supports flexible input size and
allows the user to to close choose LZ4
or ZSTD per page. Layer two is the CSD
hardware layer. It further compresses
these 4 kilobyte blocks into byte
aligned physical blocks. The variable
length FTL handles byte level indexing
without any software overhead.
Dual layer compression is the co-design
of our system. Furthermore,
since our storage only serves Polar DB,
can do many database specific
optimizations. Before going into the
details, let me first talk about the two
key IO metrics we care about. The first
one is the redo log write latency, which
is directly affects transaction commit.
The second one is the page read latency,
which affects the query performance when
we have a buffer pool miss.
Based on these two metrics, we designed
the three optimizations. The first one,
we bypass compression for redo logs. We
use a non-compression flag combined with
a high-performance SSD such as obtain
Intel obtain SSD. This works well
because redo logs are small and are
frequently recycled.
The second one, we do adaptive algorithm
selection between LZ4 and ZSTD for each
page to get better page read latency.
And the third one, we introduce a per
page log mechanism to solve the long
tail
latency problem in page read.
Let me explain the second optimization
in detail. Here is the key observation
behind the design. Because of 4 kilobyte
alignment,
even a tiny size difference between
can fill a whole IO block. Look at this
example. LZ4 compresses a page into
4,097
bytes.
That needs 8 kilobyte for all IO, but
ZSTD compresses the same page to 4,096
bytes, just one byte less, and it only
needs 4 kilobyte
IO.
That That is single byte saves 4
kilobyte IO, which easily outweighs ZSTD
higher compression higher decompression
cost. So, in this case, we use ZSTD.
But now look at the in other side. LZ4
compresses 4,095
bytes. That needs 4 kilobyte IO. ZSTD
compresses 2,000 bytes.
Also 4 kilobyte
IO. ZSTD saves zero IO here.
But it wastes the CPU on decompression.
So, in this case, we choose LZ4.
So, neither algorithm is always better.
The best choice depends on each specific
page. Our decision run per page per per
page during page writes, not on the read
path.
If CPU utilization is about 20%, we just
default to use LZ4 for lower head.
Otherwise, if the page has more than 30%
of data content, we try both algorithm
and compute the benefit to overhead
ratio. If the saved
bytes per extra microsecond
of decompression exceeds our throughput,
we pick ZSTD. Otherwise, we pick LZ4.
This threshold comes from the fact that
saving 4 kilobyte
reduces and read latency by about 20 or
14 microseconds.
Now, let me explain the third
optimization, the per page log design.
In the normal case, when a page read
arrives, the storage node reads the page
from disk in a single read.
But in the worst case, the old page
needs to be updated with new redo logs.
If these logs have been evicted from
memory and are scattered across
different locations on the disk, the
storage node needs multiple disk
disk reads.
Five or more to gather all the logs.
This causes high tail latency.
Our solution is simple. When redo logs
are about to evicted from memory, we
we proactively merge all logs belonging
to the same page into a dedicated per
page log space. Now, when a page read
arrives,
we only need two IO reads, one for the
old page and one for the per page log.
This is because we pre-merge them into
the
per page log space as a background
process.
Uh now here is a critical point of the
per page log design.
Or allocating uh extra 4 kilobyte space
for database page would
waste uh 25% of space on a normal SSD,
but the SSD compresses the unused
portions of this per page log space. So,
actually
actual physical overhead is minimal.
This optimization is only feasible with
the SSD.
Um that covers our architecture design.
Now, let me share about
what we learned from deploying it at
scale. First, the hardware redesign.
Uh on the hardware side, the first
change is the FTL.
Uh Poly Poly SSD
1 used a host-based FTL with an open
channel architecture. While this made
software iteration
easier, it caused a serious problem at
scale.
The first problem is stability. We
observed
We observed many slow IOs exceeding 1
second with some exceeding 10 seconds
and lasting more than 10 minutes.
Uh and there some kernel bugs
bring down the entire server.
Uh the second problem is the resource
consumption.
Um the host-based FTL consumed uh 184
GB of memory and the 24 CPU cores per
server for just the 25 devices.
Because of this overhead, we had to
disable software compression and limited
deployment
to only 10 devices per server.
uh Poly SSD 2 fixed all of this by
moving the
moving to a device management
FTL. This means zero uh
zero host CPU and the memory contention,
and device features are contended to
individual device rather than affecting
the entire server.
The second change is the Poly
SSD 2 is the maximizing the compression
ratio. The average hardware compression
ratio in our environment is about 2.5,
but the Poly SSD 1 only achieved a 2.4,
which led to waste
wasted physical space. To close this
gap, we need to allocate them more space
for index to achieve a higher
compression ratio.
Uh beyond host level stability, we also
encountered uh cluster level challenge.
The left finger shows the distribution
of compression ratio across the storage
nodes in a cluster.
And the right one shows the physical and
the logical space distribution.
The compression ratio varied widely for
1.2
and the two to 3.8. This created
problem. Disks become full for different
reasons.
Uh nodes with below average compression
ratio run out of physical space first,
and their logical space is wasted. Nodes
with above average compression ratio run
out of logical space first, and their
physical space is wasted because they
don't have enough index space to take
advantage of the higher compression
ratio.
In either case, uh usable capacity is
wasted.
Um to address this imbalance, we
developed a compression-aware scheduling
strategy.
Our solution is
the
as shown in this figure, we plot each
storage node with logical space
on horizontal X and physical space on
the vertical axis.
This divides nodes into four zones. Zone
A has
plenty of physical space, but limited
logical space.
Uh these are high ratio
high ratio nodes. We migrate low ratio
chunks out to the reliable and logical
pressure.
by rebalancing chunks based on their
compression ratio, we make sure both
logical and physical space are used
efficiently across the cluster.
Uh now let
let's look at the overall results in
production.
Our compressed storage have over 20,000
SSD devices managing over 100 GB of
data. In this paper, we use four
clusters in PolyDB to show the benefits
in both performance and compression
ratio. Cluster Cluster C1 used PolyDB
SSD Poly SSD 1 with software compression
disabled.
Uh Cluster C2 used PolyDB SSD 2
with all techniques enabled.
And we compared them with two normal
clusters, N1 and N2,
which used normal Intel SSD with the
same hardware setup. Cluster C2 with
Poly
Poly SSD 2 and dual layer software
compression achieved a compression ratio
of 3.55.
The cost per physical GB in 1.32,
but the effective cost per logical GB
dropped to 0.37.
This is about a 60% cost reduction
compared to normal the normal SSD.
The natural follow-up question is does
this compare hurt the performance? The
figure shows the system throughput
across the seven
workloads. C1 used Poly SSD 1 with a
hardware-only compression shows some
performance drop compared
to the uncompressed baseline N1, but the
state two
used Poly SSD 2 with dual layer
compression achieved similar performance
to uncompressed cluster N2.
Let me summarize our three key
contributions in our paper. First, the
dual layer compression that combines
software flexibility with hardware
efficiency. Second, three
database-originated
optimization targeting the two critical
IO paths uh in database.
And the third, practical lessons and
solutions from large-scale deployment.
Uh thank you for your attention.
Thank you.
